title: The EU's failure over Iceland—and Brexit
gist: Labour peer Andrew Adonis argues Iceland's narrow 52.8%-47.2% vote against EU membership failed for the same structural reason Brexit succeeded in 2016: EU leadership (Von der Leyen, Macron, Merz) refused to pre-emptively guarantee Iceland's exclusive fishing rights, just as EU leaders in 2016 refused Cameron's immigration 'emergency brake,' and warns more high-stakes EU referendums (potentially a Le Pen government in France) are coming unless the Commission changes this pattern.

themes.theme: Iceland's EU referendum result and mechanics

insights.claim: Iceland voted 52.8% against EU membership versus 47.2% in favour, a margin almost identical to the UK's 2016 Brexit vote (52% to 48%); fishing (which accounts for almost 40% of Iceland's exports) drove the 'no' vote, while fear that the US security guarantee (including the Keflavík airbase) might weaken under Trump drove the 'yes' vote.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: A near-identical referendum margin to Brexit is a striking data point that other small, resource-dependent, EU-adjacent economies (e.g. Norway, potentially future accession states) may replicate if the EU doesn't pre-emptively address their core economic sensitivity (here, fisheries) before a vote.

insights.claim: Adonis argues the outcome is not itself a crisis for European integration because Iceland is already inside the EU single market and Schengen area, so goods, fish and people can already move freely without full membership, and Finland and Sweden's recent Nato accession gives Iceland a stronger security buffer regardless of the referendum result.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Distinguishes Iceland's 'no' from a genuine rupture like Brexit -- there is no material trade/security discontinuity -- meaning markets should not price Icelandic economic disruption from this vote the way Brexit priced UK disruption.
insights.quote: This isn't another Brexit; rather, it was a vote for a fairly EU-aligned status quo.
insights.locator: paragraph on Iceland's single market/Schengen status

themes.theme: The recurring EU negotiating failure pattern

insights.claim: Adonis's central causal framework: EU leaders (Ursula von der Leyen, Emmanuel Macron, Friedrich Merz in Iceland's case; the European Commission, Angela Merkel and François Hollande in the 2016 Brexit case) repeatedly fail to make pre-emptive, decisive concessions on the single hot-button issue driving a referendum's 'no' vote -- fishing rights for Iceland, an immigration 'emergency brake' for the UK -- even though those specific concessions were not fundamentally 'impossibleist' for the EU to grant.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Identifies a repeatable, predictable EU negotiating failure mode (refusing targeted pre-emptive concessions before high-stakes referendums) that investors and policymakers can watch for as an early warning signal ahead of future EU-related votes -- if the pattern repeats, expect another 'no' surprise.
insights.locator: paragraph on three similarities with Brexit

insights.claim: Adonis argues that had Von der Leyen and other EU leaders guaranteed in advance that Icelandic fishing companies would retain sole rights to fish within Iceland's existing 200-mile exclusive economic zone, the narrow 'no' vote 'might well have been a narrow yes.'
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: A specific counterfactual claim that a single targeted policy guarantee (fishing rights) could have flipped a national referendum -- illustrates how narrow, symbolically loaded economic sectors (fishing, here analogous to steel/agriculture elsewhere) can decide binary sovereignty votes despite their small share of overall GDP.
insights.quote: Had they done this, the narrow 'no' vote might well have been a narrow 'yes.'

insights.claim: Adonis argues that had the European Commission, backed by Angela Merkel and François Hollande, granted David Cameron the immigration 'emergency brake' he sought in 2016 (including guaranteeing no automatic right for Turkish citizens to work across the EU if Turkey ever joined), the UK 'may well have voted to remain.'
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: A retrospective causal claim about the single policy concession that could have prevented Brexit -- useful historical context for assessing how the UK-EU relationship might have evolved absent Brexit, and for understanding EU institutional rigidity as a recurring self-inflicted risk factor.

themes.theme: Forward-looking risk: more EU referendums ahead

insights.claim: Adonis warns that more EU-related referendums, including some as consequential as Brexit, are inevitable, and specifically flags the scenario of a Marine Le Pen-led French government next year (2027) holding votes on new immigration controls and/or cuts to the EU budget.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Flags a specific, named forward risk (a Le Pen government triggering an EU-budget or immigration referendum in France in 2027) that would be far higher-stakes than Iceland's vote given France's size and EU centrality -- a concrete political-risk catalyst to add to any EU-fragmentation risk watchlist.

insights.claim: Adonis's prescription for the EU is that it needs 'supreme political agility' to weather coming referendums, starting with the European Commission acknowledging, with 'pragmatism and humility,' its specific past failures in the UK and Iceland cases rather than treating each vote as a one-off.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: A direct policy recommendation to EU institutions: proactively address hot-button sectoral/immigration concerns before referendums rather than after -- a template for evaluating whether the EU adapts its negotiating posture ahead of the next major vote (e.g. France 2027).
insights.quote: Supreme political agility is required if the EU is to weather them successfully.
